# Lynn Conway: Summary
Lynn Conway (1938–2024) was an influential American computer scientist and electrical engineer known for her groundbreaking work in chip design and VLSI (very-large-scale integration) methodology. After earning engineering degrees at Columbia University, Conway joined IBM in 1964, where she invented multiple-issue out-of-order dynamic instruction scheduling—a pioneering approach to computer architecture. In 1968, after beginning her gender transition, she was fired by IBM, an event for which the company later issued a public apology and awarded her a Lifetime Achievement Award.
Post-transition, Conway rebuilt her career at Memorex and then at Xerox PARC, where she co-authored the foundational textbook "Introduction to VLSI Systems" and helped develop scalable design rules and the multiproject wafers (MPW) technology. She was central to the development of the MOSIS system, which democratized access to state-of-the-art chip fabrication, fueling innovation in universities and startups. Conway held roles at MIT, DARPA (where she helped architect the Strategic Computing Initiative), and the University of Michigan, and her work triggered the Mead–Conway VLSI design revolution, shaping the electronic design automation industry and the foundry model of chip manufacturing. She was recognized with numerous awards, including induction into the National Academy of Engineering, the IEEE Computer Pioneer Award, and the National Inventors Hall of Fame.
Conway was also a prominent advocate for transgender rights, widely sharing her story beginning in 1999 and working to increase visibility and protections for transgender people within and beyond the tech industry. She coined the "Conway effect" to describe the historical marginalization of innovators from underrepresented groups. Her legacy includes transformative contributions to computing, mentoring others through her activism, and being a role model for diversity in engineering. She died on June 9, 2024, at the age of 86.
